instruction: Judge whether the rewrite preserves all substantive reasoning of the original, without omissions, unsupported additions or changes in actor, mechanism, condition, timing, scope, direction or effect. Use preserved only if all survive, changed for a material difference, uncertain if unresolved. Give specific evidence. Independently map each supplied original source passage index to the closest corresponding exact contiguous quotation in the rewrite; use null if absent. A quote can identify a changed relation; it is not a vote that the relation was preserved. Quotes are for analysis only.

Everyone tends to launch from the same bare patch. Moving the launch flags a little each week gives the grass time to grow back. Peg a bright ribbon to the top of each low fence post along the ditch so flyers looking up can still catch sight of the boundary. People taking a shortcut across the grass may never notice a line stretched in front of them. A mown path around the edge gives walkers an obvious way through.

Wind often scatters tiny clips during assembly. A shallow lipped tray on the work table keeps the fittings together until the kite is ready. Keep a current closure notice online as well as at the gate. Families transporting a long kite frame can check before making the trip on a stormy day. The small holes rabbits dig can turn an ankle when someone steps backward. Ask the opening volunteer to flag fresh holes until the grounds crew can fill them.
documents.rewrite:
Shift the launch flags a short distance each week. Flyers tend to take off from the same worn patch, and shifting the flags gives the grass there time to grow back. People cutting across the field can easily walk into a kite line they haven't seen. Mow a path around the perimeter so there's a clear route for walkers. Along the ditch, peg a bright ribbon to the top of every low fence post. That way the boundary can still catch a flyer's eye while they're looking up.

Put a shallow tray with a raised rim on the work table. It'll hold the little clips together through assembly, even when the wind picks up, until the kite is ready. Ask whoever opens the field to mark any new rabbit holes with flags. Someone walking backward could twist an ankle in one before the grounds crew gets there to fill it. Keep the closure notice up to date both at the gate and online so a family can check on a stormy day before hauling a long kite frame to the field.

Leave a gap between bookings for packing cases and folding stands. A slow pack-up then takes less time out of the next group's rehearsal. A cello endpin slides on the polished floor. Keep a few endpin stops with the chairs so cellists can play without chasing their instruments forward. Some players arrive after everyone else has begun. Giving them the door code in the booking message saves the ensemble from stopping mid-piece to let them in.

Show the accessible entrance on the booking map. The front steps can leave a player with a wheeled case searching the block for the level doorway. Store spare scores upright in folders labeled by ensemble. Loose sheets from different arrangements otherwise end up together, taking time to sort before the first piece. Put case shelves along a wall away from the doorway. Large instrument cases spread across the floor leave very little room for a late arrival to reach a seat.
documents.rewrite:
Allow time between reservations for musicians to pack their cases and fold the stands. If packing takes longer than usual, the next ensemble can still use more of its rehearsal time. Include the door code in the booking message so players arriving late can come in without making the group break off in the middle of a piece. Mark the accessible entrance on the booking map, too. A musician pulling a wheeled case who reaches the front steps shouldn't have to circle the block to find a level way in.

Give big instrument cases a home on shelves against a wall well away from the door. When cases cover the floor, a latecomer has little room to get to a seat. Keep a few endpin stops near the chairs so cellists can keep their instruments from skating forward on the polished floor. File spare scores upright and label the folders with the ensembles' names. That saves players from spending the minutes before their first piece untangling loose pages from different arrangements.

A stack by an outside shop door can soak through in one shower. A covered dispenser keeps the papers readable until someone comes for them. Ask residents to mark a small box on the signup slip if they prefer a doorstep copy. People who rarely get to the shops would still receive the bulletin. A volunteer covering an unfamiliar route may miss a shop tucked down an alley. A photograph of its entrance on the route sheet makes the handoff easier to find.

Give readers a phone number for address changes. Someone who moves within the neighborhood can keep receiving a copy, and the old doorstep stops accumulating papers. A full rack by the checkout is easy to overlook among the sale leaflets. A small sign above it telling shoppers the bulletin is free gives them a reason to take one. A holiday street closure can cut a carrier off halfway around the block. Note announced closures on the week's route map so the carrier can enter from the other end.
documents.rewrite:
Outside a shop, one shower is enough to spoil a stack beside the door. Use a covered dispenser so the bulletins will still be readable when someone picks one up. Inside, even a full rack at the checkout can get lost among the sale leaflets. A small sign above it that says the bulletin is free can persuade a shopper to take a copy.

Add a small checkbox to the signup slip for residents who prefer doorstep delivery, so the paper still reaches people who seldom get to the shops. Give readers a number to call if their address changes. When someone moves across the neighborhood, the bulletin can follow them and copies won't pile up at their former door. For the volunteer who's new to a route, add a photo of the entrance to the route sheet if a shop is tucked away down an alley. It'll help them find the handoff. Mark announced holiday street closures on that week's map as well, so a carrier can approach from the other end of the block instead of getting cut off halfway around.

Try the lamp before the families arrive. A cool-running LED that casts one clean shadow lets children handle the figures nearby and keeps the outlines easy to follow. Make a few large loop handles for children who find a narrow stick difficult to hold. They can move their own characters without an adult taking over. Let children try moving the same puppet toward and away from the lamp. Seeing its shadow grow and shrink gives them a way to turn a small character into a giant.

Give the youngest audience members cushions on the floor at the front. They can see the whole screen without having to look around adult shoulders. Put a piece of scrap card under each figure when punching holes for joints. The hole comes out clean and the hall tables stay free of dents. Invite each child to make up a different ending for a familiar tale. Knowing the characters already leaves more time to act out the new idea.
documents.rewrite:
Before the families arrive, test a cool-running LED lamp and check that it throws a single, distinct shadow. Children can handle their puppets close to the light, and the audience can follow the outlines. Offer a few large loop handles so a child who struggles to grip a thin stick can still work their character without an adult doing it for them. When punching joint holes, back each figure with a scrap of card for a neat hole and a dent-free hall table.

Let the children take one puppet closer to the lamp and farther away again to watch its shadow grow and shrink. They can use that change in size to make a little character into a giant. Invite each child to invent a different ending to a story they already know. Familiar characters leave more time to act out the new ending. Give the youngest spectators cushions on the floor at the front so they can see the entire screen without peering around adults' shoulders.

Keep a few card designs in reserve for the afternoon so late arrivals still have a choice of pictures. Print the town and today's date on a small sign at the writing places. Visitors who want to mark the occasion can copy both without interrupting a conversation. One person can write while a family debates which picture to send if the card display sits a few steps away from the writing seats.

A writer with stiff fingers may find a narrow pen tiring. Slip a wide grip onto a few pens so a longer message is comfortable to finish. A short ruler makes a good line guide on the blank side. Writers can move it down as they go and keep their lines from drifting into each other. Name a volunteer to take the collection box to the post office at closing. Cards left in the final few minutes then have someone responsible for getting them into the mail.
documents.rewrite:
Save a few postcard designs for the afternoon so the people who come later still get to choose a picture. Set the display a few steps from the seats. That leaves someone free to write while a family takes its time deciding which picture to send. At the writing places, put up a small printed sign with the town's name and today's date. Visitors can copy both onto a card to mark the occasion without breaking into anyone's conversation.

Fit a few pens with wide grips so a writer whose stiff fingers tire around a slim pen can finish a longer message comfortably. Offer a short ruler to guide the writing on the blank side of a card. Sliding it down as they write will keep one line from running into the next. Assign one volunteer to take the collection box to the post office at closing, so even the cards dropped in during the last few minutes have someone to see them into the mail.

A Saturday return still has to go through the wash. Block out drying and folding time on the booking calendar so Sunday's group is offered only what can be ready. A volunteer collecting a large wedding order may arrive on foot. Include the number of packed crates in the pickup note so they can arrange a ride if needed. Put an aisle and shelf number on each return bin. A new volunteer can then put clean linen away where the next order will be picked.

A booking for forty guests can grow after invitations go out. Set a date for the borrower to confirm the final quantity while staff still have time to adjust the order. A bag of used napkins looks much like one that never left the cupboard. Supply a separate bag for untouched spares so they can be identified on return. Put a picture of the collection door in the pickup email. First-time borrowers can go straight to the linen room even when the main hall is locked.
documents.rewrite:
Leave room on the booking calendar for drying and folding after the wash. Linens that come back on Saturday still need laundering, and Sunday's group should only be offered what will be ready. Agree on a date when the borrower will confirm the final count, early enough for staff to adjust the order. A group expecting forty can grow once the invitations have gone out.

Tell borrowers how many packed crates to expect in the pickup note. A volunteer planning to collect a big wedding order on foot can then arrange a ride if necessary. Include a photo of the collection door in the pickup email so even a first-time borrower can go straight to the linen room if the main hall is locked. Give each group a separate bag for untouched spares. You'll be able to identify the spares on return even though a bag of used napkins looks much like one that's been in the cupboard all along. Label each return bin with an aisle and shelf number so a new volunteer can put the clean linen right where the next order will be picked.

A guide who talks over a song can erase the phrase everyone came to hear. Agree on a raised hand for “listen” so the group can catch it together. The group may stretch out on a narrow path. Ask someone familiar with the route to walk last so a person who pauses to listen can find their way back to the others. Give walkers the distance and surface details in the invitation. They can decide in advance whether the full circuit works for them.

Divide a large turnout into small parties with a guide for each. People at the back can then hear the same quiet calls as those up front. Pass around a simple outline map and let people mark where they heard a song. They can return to that corner on a later walk and listen again. A busy road crossing needs everyone's attention. Finish the listening stop before the curb so the group can concentrate on getting across together.
documents.rewrite:
Put the walk's distance and the kinds of surfaces underfoot in the invitation so people can judge beforehand whether the whole circuit suits them. If a crowd turns up, send them out in smaller groups, each with a guide. A walker at the back should be able to hear the quiet calls as clearly as someone at the front. On a narrow path the party can string out. Have someone who knows the way bring up the rear so anyone who stops to listen can find their way back to the group.

Agree that a raised hand means it's time to listen. A spoken cue from the guide can drown out the very phrase everyone's trying to catch together. Pass around a simple outline map for walkers to mark the spot where they heard a song. That gives them a place to return to and listen again on another walk. If there's a busy road ahead, end the listening stop before reaching the curb so everyone can give their attention to crossing together.

Someone choosing a pen for a daily planner needs to know how it behaves on those pages. Leave room for them to try a few words in their own planner as well. Arrange the pens in shallow grooved trays. A visitor can set one down to inspect the writing without having it roll onto the floor. Have the owner refill a pen at a side table when its ink runs low. The owner knows its filling mechanism, and the writing seats stay open for the other pens.

Seat a left-handed writer at the left end of a shared table when they prefer it. Their elbow then has room to move through a line. List the ink in each pen on the sample card. Someone admiring the color can find the right bottle even if they prefer a different pen body. Ask lenders to initial their pens back out at closing. The organizer can spot a pen still waiting in its tray while its owner is nearby.
documents.rewrite:
Make space for visitors to write a few words in their own daily planners if that's where they expect to use a pen. They'll be able to see how it writes on the actual pages. At a shared table, offer a left-handed writer the left end if they'd like it, so their elbow can move freely as they write across a line. Set the pens out in shallow trays with grooves. Someone can lay a pen down to look at their writing and it'll stay put instead of rolling onto the floor.

Note the ink used in each pen on the sample card. Visitors who like a color can find the right bottle even if they'd choose a different pen body. If a pen is running low, ask its owner to refill it at a side table. They know how its filling mechanism works, and other visitors can carry on trying pens at the writing seats. At closing, have lenders initial their pens out as they collect them. The organizer can see if a pen is still in the tray while its owner is close at hand.
